title: Bone metastasis in the proximal femur: impending fracture and the Mirels score

header.contentArea: Pathology and trauma: metastatic bone disease (radiograph findings with a clinical scenario)
guidelineVersions: BOASt: Management of Metastatic Bone Disease (June 2022)
BOOS/BOA Metastatic Bone Disease: A Guide to Good Practice (2015 revision)

brief.scenario: Mrs Rosalind Tennant, 64, had breast cancer treated four years ago and was discharged from oncology follow-up. She has six weeks of right thigh pain, now worse at night and when she walks. She has not fallen. Written findings: an AP radiograph of the right proximal femur shows an ill-defined area of bone loss, darker than the surrounding bone, in the peritrochanteric region. It has eroded the lateral cortex from the inside, which is thinned to about half its normal thickness over the length of the lesion. The cortex is not breached and there is no fracture line. The femoral head and hip joint are normal.
brief.task: Interpret the written findings of her radiograph and answer questions on assessment and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Lytic lesion, stage before you fix, score the fracture risk, then plan surgery that outlasts her.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Nailing a lesion before staging. It may be a solitary metastasis or a primary bone tumour.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "A lytic lesion in the proximal right femur with cortical destruction, no fracture."

grid.label: Interprets the radiograph findings
grid.fail: Calls it osteoporosis, or plans treatment from a single view.
grid.pass: Lytic lesion in the peritrochanteric femur with cortical destruction and no fracture; wants orthogonal views of the whole femur.
grid.high: Estimates cortical involvement; notes about 50% destruction of one cortex, or lesser trochanter avulsion, signals high fracture risk.

grid.label: Pathology of bone metastases
grid.fail: Cannot name the primaries that spread to bone.
grid.pass: Breast, prostate, kidney, lung and thyroid. Prostate usually sclerotic; kidney and thyroid lytic. Breast lytic or mixed.
grid.high: Kidney and thyroid metastases are vascular: considers pre-operative embolisation. Myeloma is a key lytic differential.

grid.label: Work-up before fixing
grid.fail: Plans to nail the femur this week without bloods, staging or MDT discussion.
grid.pass: Bloods including calcium and myeloma screen; whole-femur radiographs; staging CT of thorax, abdomen and pelvis within 24 hours; MDT.
grid.high: Solitary metastasis: tertiary centre referral. Primary bone tumour features or negative staging: sarcoma centre within 72 hours, where biopsy is done.

grid.label: Mirels score
grid.pass: Site, pain, lesion type, size, each scored 1 to 3. Hers: peritrochanteric 3, functional pain 3, lytic 3, one to two thirds 2: total 11.
grid.high: Size is the maximum cortical destruction on plain film in any view; functional pain is the most important single clinical sign.

grid.label: Acts on the score
grid.pass: 9 or more: consider prophylactic fixation before radiotherapy. 7 or less: radiotherapy and observe. 8 is borderline.
grid.high: Fracture risk about 33% at 9 against 4% at 7 or less; weighs fitness, prognosis and wishes, as the score is an aid.

grid.label: Surgical plan
grid.fail: Uses a short device or plans fixation that relies on the fracture uniting.
grid.pass: Consultant-led; implant that outlasts her and allows immediate weight-bearing; cephalomedullary nail protecting the neck; post-operative radiotherapy to the whole bone.
grid.high: Curettage and cement augmentation; cemented proximal femoral replacement if destruction is extensive or prognosis good; thromboprophylaxis.

grid.label: Non-surgical treatment
grid.fail: Omits oncology input and bone-targeted treatment.
grid.pass: Oncology input; radiotherapy; bisphosphonates or denosumab to reduce skeletal-related events; analgesia; correct hypercalcaemia before surgery.
grid.high: Explains denosumab is a monoclonal antibody to RANK ligand, reducing osteoclast bone resorption.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What do the radiograph findings show?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: An AP of the right proximal femur showing a lytic lesion in the peritrochanteric region with cortical destruction. No fracture. I'd want orthogonal views of the whole femur.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Breast, prostate, kidney, lung and thyroid. Prostate is usually sclerotic, kidney and thyroid lytic, and breast lytic or mixed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She was thought cured. What next?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Bloods including calcium, bone profile and a myeloma screen, whole-femur radiographs, and a staging CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis within 24 hours. Then MDT discussion before surgery.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Staging shows several bone metastases. How would you assess fracture risk?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mirels: site, pain, lesion type and size, each 1 to 3. Peritrochanteric 3, functional pain 3, lytic 3, and one to two thirds of the cortex 2. That's 11.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: At 9 or more, consider prophylactic fixation before radiotherapy. 7 or less, radiotherapy and observe. 8 is borderline.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Consultant-led, with a cephalomedullary nail protecting the neck, so she can bear weight immediately. It must outlast her, then radiotherapy to the whole bone.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Oncology input, bisphosphonates or denosumab to reduce skeletal events, analgesia, and correct any hypercalcaemia before surgery.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you judge the cortex?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Plain films underestimate it. Destruction of about half of one cortex, or avulsion of the lesser trochanter, means a fracture is likely soon.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Anything about the primary that changes surgery?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Renal and thyroid metastases bleed, so I'd consider embolisation beforehand. And a lytic lesion always makes me think of myeloma.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What if staging shows nothing else?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A solitary metastasis goes to a tertiary centre. If staging is negative or it looks like a primary bone tumour, refer to a sarcoma centre within 72 hours, where the biopsy is done.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Maximum cortical destruction on plain film in any view. Functional pain is the most important single sign.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: About 33% at 9, and 4% at 7 or less. The score is an aid; I'd weigh her fitness, prognosis and wishes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Where internal fixation is used, curettage and cement augmentation. With extensive destruction or a good prognosis, a cemented proximal femoral replacement. Thromboprophylaxis for all.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's a monoclonal antibody against RANK ligand, reducing osteoclast resorption.

failures.move: Nailing an unstaged lytic lesion in a patient thought cured.
failures.consequence: A primary bone sarcoma is contaminated along the whole canal and limb salvage may be lost.

failures.move: Sending a high-scoring lesion for radiotherapy alone.
failures.consequence: Pathological fracture before or after radiotherapy, with emergency surgery and poorer union.

failures.move: Choosing a device that relies on fracture healing.
failures.consequence: Pathological fractures often fail to unite, so the implant fails.
Cannot justify fixation or observation to the patient or the MDT.

recovery.line: Where is it, does it hurt on use, what does it look like, and how much cortex is gone: each 1 to 3.
No fracture yet, so there's time to stage and discuss her at the MDT; I'd protect her weight-bearing meanwhile.

knowledge.fact: Primaries that spread to bone: breast, prostate, kidney, lung, thyroid.
Mirels: site, pain, lesion, size, each 1 to 3; 9 or more, consider prophylactic fixation before radiotherapy.
Suspected MBD: calcium, bone profile, myeloma screen, PSA in men; whole-bone radiographs; CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis within 24 hours.
Solitary metastasis: tertiary centre. Possible primary bone tumour: sarcoma centre within 72 hours.
Constructs should outlast the patient and allow immediate weight-bearing.

recall.think: Impending fracture, or a primary bone tumour that must not be nailed.
recall.say: "Lytic proximal femoral lesion, no fracture: stage, score, then fix."
recall.trap: A history of cancer does not make every lytic lesion a metastasis.
recall.finish: Cephalomedullary nail or cemented replacement, whole-bone radiotherapy, bone-targeted therapy.

sources.name: British Orthopaedic Oncology Society and British Orthopaedic Association. Metastatic Bone Disease: A Guide to Good Practice
sources.supports: Primaries that most often spread to bone; Mirels table and fixation at 9 or above before radiotherapy; functional pain as the key sign; 50% destruction of one cortex or lesser trochanter avulsion as high-risk signs; pre-operative embolisation for renal and thyroid metastases; cephalomedullary nails in the femur; cemented or endoprosthetic replacement around the proximal femur; whole-bone radiotherapy after nailing; bisphosphonates and denosumab; correction of hypercalcaemia

sources.name: Mirels H. Metastatic disease in long bones: a proposed scoring system for diagnosing impending pathologic fractures. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1989;(249):256–64
sources.supports: Four variables (site, pain, lesion, size) each scored 1–3; lesions scoring 7 or less can be irradiated safely; fracture risk rises with scores above 7

sources.name: Meschini C, El Motassime A, El Ezzo O, et al. Advancements in assessing pathological fracture risk: news on Mirels' score. Cancers (Basel) 2025;17(6):973
sources.supports: Mirels' original fracture risks: 4% at 7 or less, 15% at 8, 33% at 9; prophylactic stabilisation at 9 or above

Read out: staging CT shows multiple bone metastases in the spine and pelvis; no visceral disease.
Read out: pain on walking and weight-bearing, and at night.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for the lateral view
reveals.finding: Read out: the lateral view shows the lesion involves about half of the cortical width; the lesser trochanter is intact.

push.question: What would you do before any surgery?
push.expect: Bloods, whole-femur radiographs, staging CT within 24 hours, MDT.

push.question: What does the score mean for her?
push.expect: 9 or more: consider prophylactic fixation before radiotherapy.

push.question: How would you fix it?
push.expect: Cephalomedullary nail or cemented replacement; immediate weight-bearing; radiotherapy to the whole bone.

curveballs.prompt: Staging CT shows no other disease.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Do not nail. Treat as a possible primary bone tumour or solitary metastasis: sarcoma or tertiary centre referral and biopsy there.

curveballs.prompt: A 70-year-old man with prostate cancer has a sclerotic femoral lesion.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Blastic lesions score 1 for lesion type and are less likely to fracture; score it and involve oncology.
Hypercalcaemia: rehydrate and treat before surgery, with medical and oncology input.

curveballs.prompt: She falls on the ward and fractures through the lesion.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No rush to fix: splint or traction, analgesia, imaging now; plan fixation with the MDT lead.
